title: SDK client PRD — opaque-token pagination, stratified-retry semantics, streaming snapshots, and cross-language downgrade strategy
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Purpose: Define a single PRD that binds Python/TS/Go SDK behaviors for the next-gen pagination token format (opaque tokens), a stratified retry policy that preserves ordering and idempotency guarantees across languages, streaming snapshot semantics for partial responses, and a compatibility plan for progressive client downgrades and server-driven deprecations. Goal: reduce production surprises when customers upgrade or mix SDK versions and to provide clear acceptance criteria for SDK teams to implement consistent behavior across languages.
scope:
- APIs: list endpoints that return paginated data (generation logs, audit events, model catalog lists) will expose opaque continuation tokens instead of numeric cursors.
- SDKs: Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs must implement a PaginationAdapter that consumes opaque tokens, provides an ergonomic iterator/async iterator surface, and exposes token metadata for advanced users.
- Retries: implement a stratified retry helper in each SDK that classifies requests as safe/unsafe and preserves order semantics for streaming/listing endpoints.
- Streaming: define "streaming snapshot" semantics: an SDK-level buffer policy that yields stable partial events while enabling resume via snapshot tokens.
- Compatibility: supply lightweight shims so older SDKs can continue to operate with the new servers (best-effort), and provide a migration document and feature flagging for gradual rollout.
out_of_scope:
- Major API schema changes beyond opaque token exchange (no new fields added to payload bodies for this ticket).
- Non-collection endpoints (e.g., single resource GET) changes.
- Language runtimes outside Python/TS/Go.
acceptance_criteria: All three SDKs expose an idiomatic pagination primitive that abstracts opaque continuation tokens: Python -> .paginate(), TS -> for await (const page of client.paginate()), Go -> Paginate(ctx, opts) returning channel/iterator.
Opaque tokens are treated as opaque: SDKs must not attempt to parse token internals; token metadata (ttl, server_version) must be surfaced via a stable metadata object when present.

Stratified retry policy implemented: SDKs classify requests into 'idempotent', 'retriable-non-idempotent', and 'non-retriable' buckets; default: idempotent -> safe exponential backoff with jitter, retriable-non-idempotent -> single retry with server-assisted idempotency token when available, non-retriable -> fail fast and bubble error.

Streaming snapshot behavior: for streaming endpoints supporting snapshots, SDKs must provide a way to request a snapshot token mid-stream and resume from that snapshot token to receive exactly-once continuation (best-effort; documented caveats include token expiry and retention window).

Backward compatibility: When interacting with servers that return legacy numeric cursors, SDKs should wrap numeric cursors into legacy-compatible opaque tokens and maintain functional pagination for existing clients without requiring code changes.

Inter-language behavior parity: integration test harness (see linked artifacts) passes for the following scenarios: concurrent pagination + retries under partial network failures; streaming snapshot creation and resume; server returning mixed token formats (opaque and legacy) during rollout.
Performance guardrails: pagination iterator must not buffer more than 4 pages into memory by default; SDKs should expose a tunable prefetch parameter; default memory usage verified by unit tests.
Documentation and migration guide published in docs repo with code examples for Python/TS/Go, plus a deprecation timeline and recommended feature-flag rollout steps.

Telemetry: SDKs emit structured telemetry events for token format used (opaque|legacy), retry classification decisions, snapshot creation/resume attempts, and prefetch tunings (opt-in, privacy-compliant).
Security: token handling must not log token content in cleartext by default; SDKs must sample-mask token values in debug logs.
clarifications: Opaque tokens are server-generated strings containing state; SDKs must treat them as opaque and only transmit them back to server unless the server provides explicit metadata. If server provides metadata fields, SDKs expose these fields on the PageMetadata object.

Stratified retry 'retriable-non-idempotent' bucket: SDKs should attempt a single retry when an idempotency token header is supported by the server; otherwise fall back to no retry. Implementation detail left to each language’s networking layer.
Streaming snapshot retention window is configured server-side. SDKs should surface errors that indicate token expiry as a specific exception type to allow app-level retries or user-facing messages.

Compatibility shim: when older SDK versions issue numeric cursor requests, the server will reply with a synthetic opaque token and compatibility headers; SDKs must still parse and function with those responses transparently.
Telemetry collection requires explicit opt-in via client configuration (default: off).
decisions: Adopt opaque token approach to avoid exposing internal sequence IDs and to enable richer server-driven resume semantics.
Define stratified retry policy in product PRD and require language SDK owners to map policy to idiomatic retry helpers rather than enforcing identical code across languages.
Streaming snapshot API surface will be opt-in per endpoint; default behavior for streaming endpoints remains the same unless snapshot capability is advertised by server metadata.

Backwards compatibility will be prioritized: the server will accept both legacy numeric cursors and new opaque tokens during rollout window. SDKs must implement a compatibility wrapper rather than requiring server-side only support.
open_questions: What default prefetch window should we choose for high-throughput customers? (proposed default = 2 pages prefetch, max buffer = 4 pages; verify through load testing)
Should the SDK automatically attach an idempotency token for retriable-non-idempotent requests when the server advertises support, or leave this opt-in to application code?
How will token expiry errors be represented across languages to enable consistent application-level handling? (uniform exception type vs idiomatic error wrappers)
Classification of endpoints: who on product will own the authoritative list of endpoints considered 'retriable-non-idempotent' vs 'non-retriable'?
